name: PFAPA Syndrome (Periodic Fever, Aphthous Stomatitis, Pharyngitis, Adenitis)

clinicalPearls: The most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, typically beginning before the age of five.
The defining feature is highly regular, recurrent episodes of fever occurring at strikingly predictable intervals, often every 3-6 weeks.
Episodes classically combine aphthous mouth ulcers, pharyngitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy, though not every feature is present each time.
A hallmark is that the child is entirely well, thriving, and asymptomatic between episodes with normal growth and development.
It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion; recurrent streptococcal infection, cyclic neutropenia, and monogenic autoinflammatory disorders should be considered.
Fevers respond dramatically to a single dose of corticosteroid, which can be both therapeutic and supportive of the diagnosis, though steroids may shorten the interval between episodes.
Routine antibiotics are ineffective because the condition is inflammatory rather than infective.
The disorder is self-limiting, usually resolving spontaneously over several years without long-term sequelae; tonsillectomy is an option in selected cases.
reference.pathophysiology: PFAPA is regarded as an autoinflammatory disorder of innate immunity rather than an infection or classic autoimmune disease. During attacks there is dysregulated activation of the innate immune system with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling (including interleukin-1 beta pathway activity), producing the stereotyped febrile episodes. Unlike the monogenic periodic fever syndromes, no single consistent genetic cause has been identified, and inflammation resolves completely between episodes.
additionalDifferentials: Familial Mediterranean fever and other monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes
Recurrent viral infections in young children
additionalInvestigations: Documentation of the fever pattern with a symptom and temperature diary
Full blood count during and between episodes (to exclude cyclic neutropenia)
Throat swab or streptococcal testing to exclude recurrent bacterial pharyngitis
Genetic testing for monogenic periodic fever syndromes when features are atypical
Immunoglobulin levels where an alternative autoinflammatory diagnosis is suspected
redFlags: Poor growth or failure to thrive, which is not expected in PFAPA
Persistent symptoms or inflammation between episodes
Irregular, unpredictable, or evolving fever patterns suggesting another diagnosis
Neutropenia coinciding with fevers (points to cyclic neutropenia)
Features suggesting a monogenic autoinflammatory disorder such as serositis, rash, or a strong family history
reference.prognosis: Excellent; PFAPA is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving over several years with no lasting effect on growth, development, or long-term health, and it is not associated with amyloidosis or organ damage.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating episodes with antibiotics for presumed bacterial pharyngitis
Diagnosing PFAPA in a child who is unwell or failing to thrive between episodes
Overlooking cyclic neutropenia by not checking blood counts during febrile episodes
Assuming steroid responsiveness alone confirms the diagnosis without excluding mimics
Not recognising that corticosteroids may shorten the interval to the next attack
management: Abort individual febrile attacks with a corticosteroid given at the onset of an episode, which is dramatically effective and supports the diagnosis
Provide symptomatic supportive care during attacks with antipyretics or analgesia, hydration and reassurance
Consider colchicine prophylaxis in children with frequent attacks or shortened intervals between episodes
Discuss tonsillectomy as a potentially curative option in selected children with frequent or troublesome episodes
Confirm the clinical diagnosis by excluding cyclic neutropenia, recurrent streptococcal infection and monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes before committing to therapy
Counsel families that the child thrives between episodes and that the condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving over several years without organ damage
